name: data-mesh
context: Large-scale multi-domain organizations requiring decentralized data ownership where domain teams own and serve data products as first-class deliverables, with federated governance and self-serve infrastructure enabling autonomy while maintaining organizational coherence.
benefits: Domain teams own data end-to-end, accountable for quality and availability
Scales horizontally with organization growth without central bottleneck
Domain experts produce data products with proper business context
Self-serve platform reduces cognitive load on domain teams
Federated governance enables interoperability without central control
Product mindset drives quality, documentation, and SLA discipline
Fault isolation: domain failures don't cascade across organization
Faster iteration on data products with autonomous teams
Better data locality reduces cross-domain dependencies
tradeoffs: Cultural shift required: teams must think data-first, not just consume data
Federated governance complexity: balancing autonomy with standards
Significant platform investment: self-serve infrastructure is costly to build
Learning curve: domain teams need data engineering skills
Data duplication: some overlap across domains is inevitable
Cross-domain integration challenges: schema consistency, identity linking
Organizational complexity: requires clear domain boundaries and ownership
Distributed debugging: lineage tracking across domain boundaries
Reconciliation complexity: eventual consistency requires explicit handling
use_cases: Organization scaled beyond what centralized data team can support
Multiple domain teams need independent data product delivery
Data quality suffers due to central team lacking domain knowledge
Need for data agility and fast iteration on data products
Distributed architecture already in place (microservices, domain teams)
Diverse data consumers: analytics, ML, operational reporting, compliance
Cross-domain data correlation required for business insights
Real-time data needs across multiple business domains
Regulatory compliance requires clear data lineage and ownership
avoid_when: Small organization with fewer than 50 people
Single domain or simple data requirements
Centralized data team works well and satisfies stakeholders
Organization not ready for cultural shift to data-as-product
Leadership cannot support org change and domain empowerment
Budget insufficient for self-serve platform investment
Teams lack data engineering skills without upskilling path
Strong consistency requirements within single transaction boundary
component_types: Data Catalog Service: Central discovery service providing metadata, ownership registration, and search capabilities for all data products
Data Quality Monitor: Automated quality checks, SLO tracking, and alerting for data product freshness and correctness
Data Lineage Tracker: Cross-domain lineage capture and visualization enabling impact analysis and debugging across boundaries
Data Policy Engine: Federated governance rule enforcement ensuring compliance with global standards while respecting domain autonomy
Data Product Registry: Product registration, versioning, and contract management for domain data offerings
Self-Serve Platform Portal: Onboarding, provisioning, and templates enabling domain teams to build and publish without platform expertise
Schema Registry: Schema evolution and compatibility checking ensuring interoperability across domain boundaries
Identity Linking Service: Cross-domain entity resolution enabling correlation of data across domains
Reconciliation Service: Data consistency validation across domains handling eventual consistency requirements
Event Streaming Platform: Real-time data product delivery infrastructure (e.g., Apache Kafka) for low-latency domain interactions
technology_stack: Apache Kafka: Event streaming for data product delivery
Apache Flink: Stream processing and real-time transformations
Apache Iceberg: Open table format for data product storage
AWS Glue / Azure Data Factory / Google Cloud Dataproc: Data orchestration
Apache Hive Metastore / AWS Glue Data Catalog: Metadata management
dbt: Data transformation and data product definition
Debezium: Change data capture for operational data products
Prefect / Dagster: Workflow orchestration for data products
OpenPolicy Agent: Policy-as-code for federated governance
Spark / Trino / Presto: Distributed query engines
anti_patterns: Centralized data warehouse rebranded as data products
Domain teams publishing raw data without quality SLA
Tech-first bottom-up approach expecting governance to emerge
Data products as integration patterns between operational systems
Each team building own platform instead of using self-serve
Weak governance leading to schema inconsistency across domains
Data swamp with different access and security mechanisms
Consumer-specific transformations leaking into source ownership
Distributed monolith: decentralized ownership with central dependencies
design_principles: **Domain Ownership**: Teams own data for their domain end-to-end, accountable for quality, availability, and documentation
**Data as a Product**: Treat data like software product with quality standards, documentation, SLA commitments, and versioning
**Self-Serve Infrastructure**: Platform provides common capabilities (catalog, lineage, quality monitoring) reducing cognitive load on domain teams
**Federated Governance**: Global policies defined centrally but executed locally through automated enforcement
**Product Contracts**: Formal agreements between data producers and consumers specifying schema, quality, and SLA expectations
**Fault Isolation**: Domain failures don't cascade across organization; each domain operates independently
**Schema Evolution**: Backward-compatible changes with deprecation notices; schema registry enforces compatibility
best_practices: Start with pilot domain: Prove value before full organization rollout; validate approach with low-risk domain first
Invest early in self-serve platform: Platform primitives (publishing templates, schema governance, catalog integration) enable domain autonomy
Establish global standards early: Metadata models, naming conventions, schema evolution rules keep mesh coherent as it grows
Automate governance checks: Policy enforcement in CI/CD, not manual approval committees; automated compliance reduces overhead
Measure adoption and quality metrics: Track catalog coverage, data quality scores, contract test pass rates; data-driven improvement
Create "golden path" templates: Standardized patterns for new domains reduce onboarding friction and ensure best practices
Keep reconciliation as first-class concern: Eventual consistency requires explicit handling; reconciliation service prevents divergence
Define clear data product owner role: Accountability for quality, documentation, and accessibility anchors ownership
Use data contracts to make ownership operational: Schema definitions, quality standards, freshness SLAs codified in agreements
